title: Chapter 14 – A Leak We Keep
html:
[Lin Family – Lin Wenqing]

The Cleansing Talisman works the way it always works, and Lin Wenqing hates it for that.

She holds the yellow slip over the basin and feeds it a thread of green Qi, and the lines of the circuit flare once and drop their burden into the water: a soft rinse of light, a smell like rain on stone. The water in the basin turns clear and faintly warm. It has done this every morning of her life, for the bedding, the dishes, the children, the dead. A Cleansing Talisman is the cheapest thing the Lin shop sells, and it is the first one any mother learns to use.

She dips a cloth in the water, wrings it, and washes her son's face.

Bo lies on the long table in the herb-drying shed, because the main hall is full of people who want to say something to her and she cannot bear to hear it. He looks nothing like himself. Su Qinghe carried him home as though he were asleep, and he did look asleep, then. By the second night the skin has drawn tight over the bones of his face and gone the color of candle wax, and the lips have receded from the teeth, and his hands are the hands of a very old man. Sixteen years old. She counts it again on her fingers like a child. Sixteen. He was going to be seventeen at the spring festival.

She finishes his face. She does his hands. She talks to him the whole time, in the ordinary voice she has used on him since he could walk, about the weather and the state of the gourds and what she will do to him if he tracks mud into her drying shed one more time. She hears the words. She does not know where they come from.

When she is done she sets the cloth aside and lays her palm flat on his chest, over the place where the heart was, and reaches into him with the Green Pulse as she has reached into the roots of ten thousand plants.

There is nothing there. Not a thread. The Qi that fills a living body like water fills a sponge has been drawn out of him so completely that her own, when it goes in, seems to echo. He is hollow. The man in the feather cloak did not simply kill her son. He emptied him.

Wenqing takes her hand away.

"Third Aunt."

She does not turn around. She knows the footstep. Eight years old, quiet, weighted slightly to the left. The Patriarch's youngest grandson, who has a habit of arriving where he is needed a moment after anyone would have thought to look for him.

"You shouldn't be here, Jian."

"Old Hu sent me." He stops a respectful distance away. "He says to tell you the body must be burned by tonight. Not buried. He says the blood arts leave hooks. If the body stays, the hooks stay, and anyone who knows how can pull on them."

"Pull on them for what?"

"He didn't say." A pause. "He said you'd know it's true."

Wenqing closes her eyes.

She does know. It is in the last chapter of the Green Pulse Scripture, the one they teach only to alchemists: that a body emptied by a blood art keeps a thread of its owner's Qi in the marrow, like a fishhook in a trout, and a practitioner with the right art can feel the line from a hundred miles away. They had burned the wolf. They had not understood why Hu insisted.

"Then it will be tonight," she says.

She hears him take a breath, as if to say something else. She waits. He lets it out again, without a word, and comes to stand beside her, a small solemn figure with an inked left thumb and a bruise on one cheek that she does not ask about, and for a while neither of them says anything.

Then he says, "Third Aunt, I'm sorry about Bo."

"Thank you."

"He saved me the last rice ball. At the winter festival. He pretended he'd already eaten."

She turns, finally, and looks at him.

It is a strange thing to be told by an eight-year-old. It is also, she realizes, entirely true. She remembers Bo coming through the kitchen door that night with a cold rice ball wrapped in a leaf, pressing it into somebody's hands and saying he was full. She had not seen who. She had assumed it was Yue.

"He did that," she says. Her voice cracks in the middle of the sentence. "He always did that."

She puts her hand on the boy's head, briefly, the way she would for any child, and then takes it away before the grief can get into her fingers, and goes out of the shed into the cold.

\ \ \*

The pyre is built on the bare shoulder of the hill above the herb terraces, where the wind comes clean off the ridge. Fourth Uncle's guards cut the wood. Old Nan lays the bed of cypress and cedar, and weeps openly while she does it, and nobody tells her to stop.

They carry him out at dusk. The whole household comes: the Patriarch, bareheaded in the cold; Wenyuan, leaning on his sister-in-law's arm because his hands have not stopped shaking since the hollow; Su Qinghe, silent as a stone; the cousins; the guards; the mortals from the village, who have known Bo since he was a boy running errands through the lower terraces. Even Old Hu has come, hat in his hand, standing at the back with his one arm folded across his chest.

Wenqing lights the pyre herself.

She uses a Flame-Burst talisman from the shop shelf: no pepper in it, a plain one, the kind the household buys by the dozen to light its stoves. She holds it between two fingers, feeds it Qi, and sets it against the cedar at the base. The cypress catches. A thin yellow line runs up the logs and thickens, and then the whole bed is a bright standing wall of fire, and the heat is on her face, and the smoke goes up, thin and straight, into a sky full of stars.

Nobody speaks. Somewhere in the crowd, a child begins to cry and is hushed.

Wenqing watches the fire until it has burned down to the color of old copper, and then she watches the coals.

At some point in the night, she notices that her brother-in-law is standing beside her.

Lin Wenhai. Second Uncle. The family steward, the keeper of the ledgers, the man who bought her mother's funeral coffin and sent her a note afterward so she would not have to ask what it cost. He is in his good gray mourning robe, the round soft face blotched and swollen, and he is weeping, quietly, steadily, with the helpless wet-eyed look of a man who has not eaten or slept for two days.

"I am so sorry, Third Sister," he says. "So sorry. I don't have words."

She looks at him.

She knows. She has known since the spring, when Grandfather gathered the five of them in the library with the doors barred and told them what the Lin ledgers did not say. She has watched him across the breakfast table every morning since, the quick hands, the easy smile, and she has kept her face still and her mouth shut, because Grandfather asked her to. She has done it for his sake and for the family's. She has done it, heaven help her, because she was told the information he passed to the Zhao was chaff.

We feed him what we choose, Grandfather had said. A leak you know about is a weapon.

She looks at the weeping man beside her, and the weapon looks back.

"Thank you, Second Brother," she says.

His hand closes briefly on her arm. He goes away.

Wenqing stands beside the fire with her arm burning where he touched it and her son's ashes going up into the dark, and she does not scream, and she does not move, and the smoke rises.

\ \ \*

The council meets at midnight, in the library, with the doors barred.

There are only six at the table. Grandfather at the head, white-faced, one hand flat on the wood. Wenyuan across from him, hollow-eyed. Fourth Uncle in his armor, the guard captain's cloak still on his shoulders. Su Qinghe, upright and quiet. Old Hu, by special leave, in the corner chair with the iron rod across his knees.

And Wenqing, at the foot, with her hands folded in her lap like a woman at prayer.

"Second Brother is not here," she says.

"No," says Grandfather.

"Why?"

"Because this meeting is about him."

She waits. The lamp hisses. The old man lays something on the table between them, a thin sheet of paper covered in his careful hand, and slides it down the wood toward her.

She reads it. It takes a long time. The words do not stay still.

Date of hunt: sixth day of the second month. Route: north trail, charcoal-burners' hut. Party: Mao, Feng, Bo, Shu. Told to W.: all of it, true. Reason: the false date was set for the herb trip on the fourteenth. He has never been told the real plan for the fourteenth. Zhao did not move on the false date. Therefore W. told Zhao of the sixth.

At the bottom, in the same hand, smaller:

My error. I thought Zhao would send men to take the herbs. I did not think he would send a demon.

"It was a trap," Wenqing says slowly. "The herb trip. You laid a false date for him to carry, and he didn't carry it. He carried the real one."

"He carried the real one because I did not think of the hunt as something he'd bother to sell. A hunt for blood." Grandfather's voice is level. His hand, on the table, is not. "I made two traps, Wenqing. I forgot he could walk into a third."

"My son is dead."

"Yes."

"You are telling me that you knew."

"I am telling you that I knew he was selling us. I did not know what he would sell." The old man looks at her without flinching. It is, she thinks, the worst thing about him: he never flinches. "I will say this once, and I will not ask you to forgive it. I put a lure in the water, and a shark took your son."

The lamp hisses.

Wenqing sits very still. She finds that she has stood up, without deciding to, and that her chair has gone over behind her with a crack.

"Then take him down," she says. Her voice is low and quite steady. "Take him down the forty steps tonight. Now. You have the law. You have the right. He sold us to a man who drinks children. Take him to the chamber and be done with it."

Nobody moves.

"That is what Father would have done," says Fourth Uncle quietly. "Before the law was a thing we had to hold."

"Then it should be done."

"It can't be," says Wenyuan.

His voice is gentle. It is the voice he uses on the children, on the dying, on the customers who come to the shop to haggle. She turns on him with a hatred so sudden that it frightens her.

"Because?"

"Because there is no proof," says her brother-in-law. "Not proof that a council can hold."

She stares at him.

"Our law says a clan member who sells his clan to its enemy is judged by the full council, before witnesses, on proof." He lays one hand over the other. "We all know he did it. That is not proof. If we take him down the stairs tonight, on knowledge, then Zhao Heng petitions the Outer Affairs Hall in the morning that the Lin Patriarch has murdered his own son in the dark without trial, and the Hall sends an arbiter, and the arbiter asks to see the evidence. And we have none."

"We have a paper in my father's handwriting."

"We have an old man's speculation about a date." Wenyuan's smile is thin and terrible. "Proof is what Wenhai took care to make sure we would never have. He has a Silent Jade Box. A gift from Zhao, I believe. It seals whatever is inside it against any spiritual scan. His letters, his tallies, his meetings, everything we would need. It is in his rooms, or on his body, or buried somewhere in the hill, and we cannot see it, and we cannot find it, and if we open his rooms without cause, we hand Zhao the same petition."

"Then break the box."

"It's a Relic," says Hu, from the corner, without looking up. His voice is rough. "Yellow grade, by the sound. A sealed container. You can break it, but the seal will burn what's inside the moment it cracks. Everything he's got in it would go up in smoke, and it would be a clean fire." He shrugs his one shoulder. "Zhao picked his tools well."

Wenqing looks around the table. Grandfather, grim. Wenshi, with his jaw set. Su Qinghe, whose eyes meet hers and do not look away.

"There is more," says Grandfather.

"There is always more."

"He is owed nothing by this family," says the old man. "But this family owes him, and his father before him, and most of the cousins at this table. You know the figures better than I do. Over six years, Wenhai has lent the stones of the clan treasury to five of the side branches. The Maos, the Shus, the Kais, the Dongs, the Tangs. Money to buy seed in a bad year, to bury a father, to marry off a son. They owe it to him, personally, on the treasury's books. If he were taken down the forty steps on suspicion, five households would be told their debts were void, and then told to guess whether their own names were in his box too."

"That's a threat," says Wenqing.

"It is a fact." Grandfather's eyes are tired. "He built himself a wall of favors, Wenqing. Brick by brick. Every cousin at that table, and every cousin who is not, owes him something. We could pull that wall down tonight with our hands. But it would fall on all of us."

She sits down. Slowly. Su Qinghe, without a word, rights the chair behind her.

"And the other thing," Wenyuan says. "The thing that is true no matter what we do."

"Say it."

"If we take him now, before the Foundation Establishment pill, Zhao knows we have turned. He knows we know. He will stop being patient." Her brother-in-law's eyes meet hers. "Right now, Zhao thinks we are fools. That is the thing keeping the hill standing, Wenqing. A man who thinks his prey is blind does not hurry. If we tell him we can see him, he will hurry. And Father is not yet ready."

"Then my son died for a pill."

Silence.

"Your son died," says Grandfather, "because I used the wrong lure. The pill is a different thing. The pill is the reason I will not make the same mistake twice." He stands, slowly, and looks down at her from his full height, an old man with white hair and an iron spine. "Here is what I propose, and I want you to hear it, and then I want you to vote against it if you can."

"Go on."

"We keep him. We keep him where we can see him. We feed him nothing true again, not one word, not the weather. And we find the proof. We find the box, or we find another way to the same truth, and when we find it, we bring him to this table and judge him before the whole clan, before witnesses, under the law. Openly. In daylight. With no petition for Zhao to write." His voice drops. "And when that day comes, Wenqing, I will give you the first word."

She looks at him for a long time.

She thinks of her son's hollow chest. She thinks of the chamber at the bottom of the forty steps, which she has seen only once, as a girl, and which she has never wanted to see again. She thinks of a round-faced man weeping beside the fire, with his hand on her arm.

Proof, she thinks. It is a bitter, colorless little word, and it has Bo's death in it.

"I will not vote against it," she says.

The old man lets out a breath that she realizes he has been holding for a very long time.

"But I want one thing," she says.

"Name it."

"The first word is mine. Not as a courtesy. As a right. When the day comes, I speak first, and I say what I like, and no one in this room stops me."

"Done," says Grandfather.

"On the record."

"On the record." Wenyuan has a brush and a sheet of paper in his hands already. His writing hand trembles, but the characters come out clear. He signs. One by one, they sign. Wenqing signs last, and presses her thumb to the ink, and leaves a print on the page that is smaller than she expected.

\ \ \*

She does not go to bed.

She goes instead to the alchemy room at the back of the herb terraces, a low stone building with a tiled roof and a single iron-bound door, and lights the lamp. The room smells of a hundred things at once: dried mugwort, camphor, the sharp green of fresh heart-root, the sweet brown scent of old resin. On the long bench stands her cauldron.

It is a modest thing, a copper tripod the height of her knee, black on the inside, scored on the lip by thirty years of use. A Yellow-grade vessel, her late husband's wedding gift, bought from a Sect merchant who has been dead for twenty years. It is not a good cauldron. It runs hot on one side, and the spirit-fire it holds will do nothing hotter than a middling Grade 2 pill. She has made some five hundred Breath-Gathering Pills in it, and a few hundred Clear Poison, and a Grade 3 Marrow Pill, once, on a good day, with a great deal of luck.

That is the sum of her art. A Qi Refining alchemist at the fourth layer, with a Yellow cauldron and a patient hand.

She has never before wished it were more.

She hears the door open behind her, softly, and does not turn.

"I made it up," says a small voice. "The part about the rice ball."

Wenqing's hands stop on the bench.

"I didn't see him," says Lin Jian. "I just thought, if someone were going to say something kind about Bo, that would be it. I'm sorry. I didn't think. I shouldn't have said it as if I'd seen it."

For a long moment she doesn't answer. Then she turns, and looks at him, and he is standing just inside the door with his hands at his sides and an expression on his thin face that she has no name for. Not guilt. Something harder than that. It is the look of a very young boy who has realized that he made a mistake in front of someone he trusts, and has made up his mind to say so and bear whatever follows.

"It was true," she says.

"I—"

"Bo did it for years. I don't know whose rice ball it was. I know he did it." She sets down her hands. "You don't have to be sorry for being right."

He swallows. "Yes, Aunt."

"What do you want, Jian? It's the middle of the night."

"I wanted to give you this."

He crosses the room and puts something on the bench beside the cauldron. A small stoppered jar of pale green glass, no bigger than her thumb. She picks it up and tilts it toward the lamp. Inside is a thin, grainy powder, the color of dust.

"What is it?"

"Dried willow-mint, from Old Hu's bath. I thought it might help you sleep."

She unstops it. A faint clean scent, wintergreen and something cooler, rises into the air. She tips a pinch onto her palm and looks at it without really seeing it, and then she does see it.

The grains are uniform. Perfectly uniform. Each one is the same size as its neighbors, with the same pale glint, no dust, no fiber, no stray fleck of bark. She has ground herbs for thirty years. She has never in her life made a powder like this. She wouldn't have thought it possible without a stone mill and a week.

She looks up at her nephew.

"Where did you get this?" she asks, very gently.

"I made it."

"How?"

He is silent. His eyes do not move from hers. It occurs to her that he has stood in front of the Patriarch in just this way, and in front of Old Hu, and in front of his father, and that every one of them has stopped asking after a moment, because the thin, inky, bruised-faced boy in front of them simply waits, and nothing at all comes out.

There is something he cannot tell me, she thinks. There is something he will not.

She has been a widow for eleven years and a mother for sixteen. She knows the look.

"Jian," she says. "I saw what you did for Feng. I saw you with your hand on the poultice. I was not sure what I was seeing, and I am still not. I am not going to ask." She closes the jar and holds it in her fist. "But whatever it is, I want you to hear this. Whatever you are doing, whatever you can do, if there is anything I can give you, anything at all, an herb, a recipe, this room, you ask me. You understand? You do not do it alone."

He is very still.

"Bo is gone," says Wenqing. "I will not spend the next ten years burying children. If there is something you can do to make the hill safer, I will help you do it. Whatever it costs me."

"Thank you, Aunt," says Lin Jian. His voice is rough.

"Go to bed."

"Yes."

At the door he hesitates. "Aunt. The clear-poison pill. The one with the heart-root and the frost-cap. Is it a Grade 2 or a Grade 3?"

"Two," she says, surprised. "Why?"

"I think," says the boy slowly, "that if you added a third of a measure of salt-bark, it might be a Three. The frost-cap is carrying too much of the load. The salt-bark would take some of it off. I've been reading your notes."

He bows, and goes out, and shuts the door behind him.

Wenqing sits for a long time in the lamplight with the jar in her hand.

\ \ \*

She does not know what makes her check the gift.

It is the habit of a decade, probably: the herbalist's instinct to look twice at anything that comes to the door. Hours later, when the lamp has burned low, she goes through the little pile of mourning gifts that the household left on the shelf by the door. A basket of eggs from the village. A bundle of incense. A cake of the good resin from Fourth Uncle. And a jar of wine, wrapped in gray cloth, with a note in a neat round hand.

For Bo, with deepest sorrow. — W.

She turns it over. The wax at the neck is dark green, unblemished, and stamped with the clan seal, which means he asked the steward's clerk for a clean stamp. A careful man. A man who does not leave a mark he can't account for.

But the wax has a flaw. It is a tiny thing, at the base, a flake no bigger than a grain of rice where the stamp pulled free. And beneath the flake, caught in the seam of the glaze, is a speck of red lacquer.

She picks at it with a needle.

It comes away in a sliver. A scrap of the underside of a gambling chip, red lacquered wood, with a corner of a gold character still attached. She turns it to the lamp.

Nine, it says, in the old script. And below, half-cut: Dice.

For a long time she does not move. A drunk's token, from a drunk's house. A man who wraps a jar in cloth for the dead and doesn't notice the chip stuck under the glaze. The kind of mistake no careful man makes. The kind that every careful man makes eventually, at the end of two bad nights.

It is not proof. A scrap of lacquer is not what the council will hold. She knows that. Wenyuan would say so; Grandfather would say so; the arbiter would laugh.

But it is a thread.

She takes the sliver and wraps it in a square of clean paper, and writes beside it, in her small, steady hand, the date and the hour and the name of the jar. Then she opens the lid of the little cedar box that sits on the shelf above her cauldron, the box where she has kept Bo's milk teeth for sixteen years, and lays the paper inside, beneath them, where nobody will look.

The first word is mine, she thinks.

She closes the lid. The lamp gutters. Outside, over the dark hill, the first gray of morning is just beginning to show, and she sits very straight in her chair and waits for it with open eyes.
